As Javanese court music developed and changed, the making of kempul was gradually refined. In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, when the West became interested in Eastern music, the gamelan and its instruments — the kempul among them — began to reach European and American musical circles. Today the kempul is a symbol of Indonesia's traditional musical culture and is widely used in local religious rites, court performance and folk music.

The kempul is a hanging gong used in Indonesian gamelan, an idiophone with the Hornbostel–Sachs number 111.241.11. It is a set of tuned gongs with a raised central boss, usually made of bronze, wood and rope, measuring about 19 to 25.4 cm across; the player strikes the boss with a soft-headed wooden mallet with a short handle and a thick round padding. In an ensemble five are commonly hung on one frame, alongside the larger Gong ageng and gong siyem; it is used in the gamelan traditions of central and eastern Java, where it helps to divide the musical structure.

Gamelan music is a treasure of Javanese traditional culture with more than a thousand years of history, and the kempul arose with it. This hanging struck gong is made of bronze, measures between 19 and 25.4 cm across, has a flat face with a raised boss at the centre, and is played with a soft-headed wooden mallet.

The source states only that it is usually made of bronze, wood and rope; the sounding body is the bronze face with its central boss, and the hanging parts are probably wood and rope, though this is not itemised. The mallet is wooden, with a round, thickly padded head on a short handle. The source does not state the alloy of the face, or the materials of the frame and the padding.

In the central Javanese pieces Ayak-ayakan, Srepegan and Sampak the kempul has a fixed metric relationship with the kenong; older East Javanese ensembles usually had a single kempul, and many later ensembles have three or four in each tuning system.
克姆普爾鑼的音色溫潤而富有穿透力，帶有明亮的金屬質感，敲擊時能迅速達到峰值，隨後: The kempul's timbre is warm and penetrating, with a bright metallic ring; struck, it reaches its peak quickly and then decays. Its range lies in the upper middle register, and because each gong has a different pitch, the whole set forms a rich combination of intervals. Struck with the heavy, round-headed wooden mallet, the kempul produces a deep yet clear resonance, lasting and full. Compared with the heavy, dull sound of a large bronze gong, the kempul is brighter and more buoyant; compared with the metallophone, its tone is warmer. In the gamelan the kempul is often a marker of the phrase, and its particular resonance answers the other percussion, building a texture of many layers.
